lessons.title: What Affiliate Marketing Actually Is
objectives: Explain the full chain from a click on your link to money in your bank account, including the steps where it can break
Work out the realistic monthly earnings of an audience the size of yours, using click-through and conversion rates instead of hope
Say why most affiliate accounts earn nothing, and name the two numbers that decide whether yours will
lessons.notes:
Affiliate marketing is simple to describe and hard to do. A company gives you a link that identifies you. Somebody clicks it, buys something, and you get a cut. That is the whole idea. Everything difficult about it lives in the gap between those sentences.

HOW THE LINK ACTUALLY WORKS

Your link is an ordinary web address with your ID attached to the end. When somebody clicks it, the shop drops a small file called a cookie on their device that says "this visitor came from affiliate 48127". If they buy before that cookie expires, the sale is credited to you.

That expiry is called the COOKIE WINDOW, and it varies wildly:

- Jumia: typically 7 days
- Most software companies: 30 to 90 days
- Amazon Associates: 24 hours

Read the window before you join anything. A 24-hour window means a reader who thinks it over for a weekend earns you nothing.

THE COOKIE BREAKS MORE OFTEN THAN COMPANIES ADMIT

The cookie is stored on ONE browser on ONE device. So you earn nothing when:

- A reader clicks on your link in the Facebook in-app browser, then reopens the shop in Chrome to buy
- A reader clicks on their phone and buys later on a laptop
- A reader clears their browser data, or browses in private mode
- A reader clicks somebody else's affiliate link after yours, and the shop pays the LAST click
- A reader goes straight to the shop the next day without your link at all

None of that is your fault, and none of it earns you anything. This is why real conversion rates are much lower than the numbers in affiliate marketing adverts.

THE CHAIN, WITH THE NUMBERS THAT MATTER

Four things have to happen in order:

1. Somebody sees your post. Call that your REACH.
2. They click your link. The share who do is your CLICK-THROUGH RATE. For honest, relevant recommendations this is often 1 to 5 percent. For a link dropped into a group of strangers it can be under 0.5 percent.
3. They buy. The share of clickers who buy is the CONVERSION RATE. For physical goods on a Kenyan marketplace, 1 to 3 percent is normal. Expensive items are lower.
4. The sale sticks. Returns, cancellations and fraud checks all reverse commissions, usually 30 to 60 days later.

Multiply those together and the picture gets honest fast.

A WORKED EXAMPLE, WITH REAL KENYAN NUMBERS

Say you have 2,000 followers and one post reaches 400 of them.

- 400 see it
- 3 percent click: 12 clicks
- 2 percent of clicks buy: 0.24 sales

So one post to 400 people produces roughly one sale every four posts. If the average order is KSh 3,000 and the commission is 7 percent, that sale pays KSh 210. Across four posts, that is about KSh 52 per post.

That is not a reason to quit. It is the reason the people who earn from this treat it as a volume-and-intent problem: either many more people see each post, or the people who see it are much closer to buying. Those are the only two levers. Everything in this course is one of those two.

WHY MOST AFFILIATE ACCOUNTS EARN NOTHING

The commonest failure is not laziness. It is applying a strategy built for a different situation:

- Links shared with friends and family, who are not in the market for the product
- Links for products that cannot be delivered to the reader
- A niche with no recurring buying need, so one sale is the ceiling
- Giving up at month two, when search traffic takes four to six months to build
- Picking a programme that cannot pay a Kenyan account, which we deal with in lesson 3

GETTING PAID IS A SEPARATE PROBLEM FROM EARNING

Earning a commission and receiving it are two different events. Every programme has a PAYOUT THRESHOLD, a minimum balance before it sends anything, and a PAYMENT SCHEDULE, usually 30 or 60 days after the month closes.

Local programmes such as Jumia pay in shillings to a Kenyan bank account, which is the simplest case. International programmes usually pay in dollars through PayPal or a bank transfer, with a threshold of 50 to 100 dollars. If you earn 12 dollars a month from an international programme with a 100 dollar threshold, you wait eight months for your first payment, and transfer fees take a bite when it arrives.

Check the threshold and the payment method BEFORE you build an audience around a programme, not after.

WHAT THIS IS GOOD FOR, AND WHAT IT IS NOT

Affiliate marketing works well as a second income stream on top of something you already do: a review channel, a how-to blog, a niche WhatsApp community you already run, a YouTube channel about a specific skill. It pays you for recommendations you were going to make anyway.

It works badly as a from-zero plan to replace a salary this quarter. Nothing about the maths above supports that, and anyone who tells you otherwise is usually selling you a course rather than showing you their payout statements.
lessons.practice:
Work out your own numbers instead of borrowing somebody else's.

Step 1. Pick the audience you actually have right now. A WhatsApp group you run, your Instagram followers, a Facebook page, a YouTube channel, or the people who read your blog. Write down the real number. If it is 60 people, write 60.

Step 2. Estimate your reach per post. On most social platforms, a post reaches 10 to 30 percent of your followers. In a WhatsApp group, nearly everybody sees it. Write your honest number.

Step 3. Pick a product your audience would plausibly buy and look up its price on Jumia or Kilimall. Write the price.

Step 4. Fill in this calculation, writing every line:

- Reach per post: ____
- Clicks at 3 percent: ____
- Sales at 2 percent of clicks: ____
- Product price: KSh ____
- Commission at 7 percent: KSh ____
- Earnings per post: sales x commission = KSh ____
- Posts needed to reach KSh 1,000: ____

Step 5. Now answer two questions in writing:

- At your current audience size, how many posts a month would KSh 5,000 require? Is that a number of posts you could actually publish?
- Which is easier for you over the next three months: multiplying your reach, or finding readers who are much closer to buying?

Keep this page. In lesson 6 you will compare it against what you really earned, and the gap will teach you more than any guide.

quiz.question: A reader clicks your affiliate link on their phone, thinks about it for two days, then buys on their laptop without using your link. What happens to your commission?
options: You still earn it, because the cookie window was 7 days
You earn nothing, because the cookie was stored on the phone browser only
You earn half, split with the shop
You earn it once you report the sale to the programme

quiz.question: You have 500 followers, a post reaches 150 of them, 3 percent click and 2 percent of clickers buy a KSh 4,000 item paying 7 percent commission. Roughly what does that post earn?
options: About KSh 25
About KSh 280
About KSh 1,200
About KSh 4,000

lessons.title: Choosing Your Niche
objectives: Define a niche as a specific person with a repeated, paid problem, rather than as a product category
Check that a niche can actually pay you from Kenya before you spend months building for it
Score three candidate niches against commission value, buying frequency and your own ability to keep writing about them
lessons.notes:
A niche is not a product category. "Phones" is not a niche. "Choosing a first smartphone under KSh 15,000 for a parent who mostly uses WhatsApp and M-Pesa" is a niche, because it names a person, a budget, and a decision they are stuck on.

The reason the specific version works is intent. Somebody searching "best phone" is browsing. Somebody searching "best phone under 15000 in Kenya with good battery" has already decided to buy and is choosing between two or three options. Your recommendation can change that decision. That is where affiliate commission comes from.

THE THREE QUESTIONS THAT KILL BAD NICHES EARLY

Before anything else, ask these in order. Most ideas die at question two or three, which saves you months.

1. CAN IT PAY ENOUGH PER SALE?

Commission per sale is price multiplied by rate. Both matter.

- Phone accessories: KSh 800 item at 8 percent is KSh 64 a sale. You need 80 sales for KSh 5,000.
- Laptops: KSh 60,000 item at 4 percent is KSh 2,400 a sale. Two sales is KSh 4,800.
- Web hosting: a 40 dollar plan at 40 percent is about 16 dollars, roughly KSh 2,000, and some hosts pay a flat 60 to 100 dollars for a referral.

Low-priced goods are not disqualified, but they demand far more traffic. Be honest about which problem you would rather have.

2. DO PEOPLE BUY IN IT REPEATEDLY?

One-off purchases mean every shilling requires a brand new reader. Recurring needs mean the same reader can earn for you several times.

- One-off: a laptop, a fridge, a wedding dress
- Recurring: skincare, baby supplies, printer ink, gym supplements, software subscriptions, hair products, farming inputs

A recurring niche also makes an email list or WhatsApp broadcast worth building, because the same people come back.

3. CAN IT ACTUALLY PAY A KENYAN ACCOUNT?

This is the question most guides skip, and it wastes the most time. Before committing, open the programme page and confirm three things:

- Does the programme accept applicants in Kenya at all?
- How does it pay? Bank transfer in shillings, PayPal in dollars, or a store credit you cannot spend?
- What is the payout threshold, and how long would your realistic earnings take to reach it?

A genuine example of this trap: Amazon Associates pays United States affiliates in various ways, but for many non-United States affiliates the practical options are a cheque or an Amazon gift card, with a 100 dollar threshold. Writing Amazon reviews for a Kenyan audience adds a second problem on top: most readers cannot easily buy and receive the item anyway. The traffic converts badly and the payout is awkward. Both problems were visible on the programme page before you started.

THE DELIVERY TEST

Your reader has to be able to receive the thing. Check:

- Is it on a shop that delivers to your readers, including outside Nairobi?
- What does delivery cost compared to the item? A KSh 600 item with KSh 400 delivery to Kisumu will not convert.
- Is it a digital product, where delivery is instant and location does not matter?

Digital products, software and online services sidestep delivery entirely, which is one honest reason they are a good starting niche from Kenya.

THE THIRTY POST TEST

Can you write thirty genuinely useful things about this niche without repeating yourself or inventing facts?

If you cannot, you do not have a niche, you have a single post. Thirty is roughly what it takes before search traffic becomes a steady trickle rather than an accident. List at least ten of the thirty titles before you commit. If the list is a struggle at six, pick something else.

WHERE YOUR OWN KNOWLEDGE COUNTS

Readers can tell the difference between somebody who has used a product and somebody who has read the specification sheet. First-hand knowledge is the cheapest advantage you have, and it is the hardest for a competitor to copy.

So weigh your own experience heavily. A niche you know nothing about but which pays well is a niche where you will be writing guesses, and guesses do not earn trust or repeat readers. If you have been a tailor for six years, sewing machines and fabric sourcing is a stronger starting niche than cryptocurrency, whatever the commission tables say.

TOO BROAD AND TOO NARROW

Too broad looks like "technology". You are competing with every publisher on the internet and you have nothing specific to say.

Too narrow looks like "replacement screens for one discontinued phone model". There is not enough search demand to sustain thirty posts.

The workable middle usually has a shape like this: SPECIFIC PERSON plus SPECIFIC DECISION plus SPECIFIC CONSTRAINT. "Budget sewing machines for tailors starting a home business in Kenya." "Accounting software for a Kenyan small business that needs to file with KRA." "Second-hand laptops for university students under KSh 30,000."

PICK ONE AND STAY FOR SIX MONTHS

The commonest mistake after choosing badly is choosing constantly. Search traffic compounds slowly, and every switch resets the clock. Choose with the questions above, then give it six months of real work before you judge it.
lessons.practice:
Score three niches properly instead of picking one by feel.

Step 1. Write down three candidate niches, each in the specific form: a person, a decision, and a constraint. Not "beauty" but "affordable skincare for oily skin in a humid coastal climate".

Step 2. For each one, research and record these facts. Do not guess any of them, look them up.

- A typical product and its real price on Jumia, Kilimall or the vendor site
- The commission rate the programme advertises
- Commission per sale in shillings: price x rate
- Buying frequency: one-off, or how many times a year
- Payment method to Kenya: shillings to bank, dollars to PayPal, or none
- Payout threshold, and months it would take you to reach it at a realistic ten sales a month

Step 3. Score each niche out of 5 on four lines, and add up:

- Commission per sale: 5 if above KSh 1,000, 3 if KSh 200 to 1,000, 1 if below KSh 200
- Repeat buying: 5 if several times a year, 3 if yearly, 1 if once in a lifetime
- Pays Kenya cleanly: 5 if shillings to a bank, 3 if PayPal in dollars, 1 if awkward or unavailable
- Your own experience: 5 if you have used these products yourself, 1 if you would be guessing

Step 4. For the highest scoring niche, list ten post titles you could write usefully. Each must answer a question somebody would actually type.

Step 5. If you cannot reach ten titles without strain, score the second niche instead. Write one sentence explaining which niche you chose and which of the four scores decided it. Date the page. In six months it will tell you whether your judgement was right.

quiz.question: Which of these is a workable niche rather than a category or a single post?
options: Electronics
Replacement screens for one discontinued phone model
Second-hand laptops under KSh 30,000 for university students
Online shopping

quiz.question: A programme in your chosen niche pays 40 percent commission but only via a method unavailable to Kenyan accounts, with a 100 dollar threshold. What is the right conclusion?
options: Join anyway, because a high commission rate outweighs payment problems
The commission rate is irrelevant until the money can reach you, so find a programme that pays Kenya or change niche
Build the audience first and solve payment later
Use a friend abroad to receive the payments

lessons.title: Joining a Real Affiliate Program
objectives: Compare the affiliate programmes genuinely open to a Kenyan applicant on commission, cookie window, payment method and threshold
Prepare an application that gets approved, and recognise the four reasons applications are rejected
Build and test a tracked affiliate link, using subIDs so you can tell which post earned the sale
lessons.notes:
Most affiliate programmes are free to join and take a few minutes to apply to. The work is choosing the right one and preparing an application that does not get refused.

WHAT IS GENUINELY AVAILABLE FROM KENYA

Programme terms change, so verify each of these on the programme page before you apply. Treat the figures below as the shape of the market, not as today's guaranteed rates.

LOCAL MARKETPLACES

- Jumia Affiliate Programme. The most practical starting point for physical goods. Commission is typically in the single digits and varies by category, the cookie window is short, and it pays in shillings to a Kenyan account. Low rate, but the entire chain works: your reader can buy, receive the item, and you can be paid.
- Kilimall and other regional marketplaces run similar schemes with similar economics.

The honest trade-off with local marketplaces is a low commission rate on mostly low-priced goods. You need real traffic volume for this to add up.

INTERNATIONAL SOFTWARE AND SERVICES

- Web hosting and domain companies, design and productivity tools, online course platforms, and VPN services all run affiliate programmes that accept Kenyan applicants and usually pay via PayPal or bank transfer in dollars.
- Commission is far higher, often 20 to 50 percent, or a flat fee per signup. Cookie windows are usually 30 to 90 days.
- The product is digital, so delivery and shipping costs disappear.

The trade-off here is that payment arrives in dollars with a threshold, usually 50 to 100 dollars, and you will lose some of it to conversion and transfer fees.

AFFILIATE NETWORKS

A network hosts many programmes behind one account and one payout, which means one threshold instead of five. Some accept Kenyan publishers, some do not. The advantage is consolidated payment and reporting; the disadvantage is that approval is usually stricter because you are applying to the network and then to each advertiser inside it.

WHAT TO CHECK BEFORE YOU APPLY, EVERY TIME

Write these six facts down for any programme before you join:

1. Commission rate, and whether it differs by product category
2. Cookie window in days
3. Payment method available to a Kenyan account
4. Payout threshold and payment schedule
5. What VOIDS a commission: returns, cancellations, self-purchases, a reader using a coupon code from elsewhere
6. Whether paid advertising on the brand name is allowed, because bidding on a brand term is a common reason for being removed

If any of the six is not stated on the programme page, ask support before building anything on it.

APPLYING WITHOUT GETTING REJECTED

Programmes ask where you will promote their products, and they check. The four common rejection reasons are all avoidable:

- AN EMPTY SITE OR CHANNEL. A blog with two placeholder posts gets refused. Publish five to ten genuinely useful posts in the niche FIRST, then apply. This single step is the difference for most first-time applicants.
- NO CLEAR TRAFFIC STORY. "I will share on social media" is not an answer. "I run a 2,000 member WhatsApp community for tailors in Nakuru and publish weekly buying guides" is.
- MISMATCHED CONTENT. Applying to a baby products programme with a gaming channel.
- MISSING BASICS. No contact page, no about page, no privacy policy if you collect emails. These take an hour and remove a whole class of refusal.

When you apply, be accurate about your audience size. Inflating it does not help, because the programme sees your real traffic within a month.

GETTING AND BUILDING YOUR LINK

Once approved, your dashboard gives you either a ready-made link or a tool that turns any product page into a tracked one. The link contains your affiliate ID.

Then do the thing most beginners skip: use SUBIDS. Most programmes let you add your own label to a link, so the dashboard reports it back to you. It looks like adding a parameter such as subid=whatsapp-oct or subid=sewing-guide to the end of your link, with the exact parameter name given in the programme documentation.

This matters enormously. Without subIDs you will know you made four sales. With subIDs you will know all four came from one blog post and none from the three weeks you spent posting on Instagram. That is the difference between guessing and managing.

TEST EVERY LINK BEFORE YOU PUBLISH IT

Links break silently, which means you lose sales without any error to warn you. Before publishing:

1. Open the link in a private or incognito window.
2. Confirm it lands on the right product, not a homepage or a 404 page.
3. Confirm the address bar shows your affiliate ID surviving any redirects.
4. Check the programme dashboard an hour later and confirm the click was recorded.

Do this again any time you change your site, move to a new link shortener, or notice clicks arriving with no sales for an unusually long stretch.

KEEP A RECORD OF WHAT YOU JOINED

Within a year you will have accounts on several programmes, each with its own login, threshold, payment method and rules. Keep one page listing each programme, your affiliate ID, the login email, the threshold, the payment method, and the date you joined. You will need it when a payment goes missing and nobody remembers which account it belonged to.
lessons.practice:
Join one programme properly and set up tracking you can trust.

Step 1. Choose one programme that fits the niche you scored in lesson 2. One, not four. Managing a single programme well teaches more than five half-set-up accounts.

Step 2. Before applying, record the six facts on one page: commission rate, cookie window, payment method to Kenya, payout threshold and schedule, what voids a commission, and whether brand-term advertising is allowed. Copy them from the programme page, not from a blog about the programme.

Step 3. Make yourself approvable. If your site or channel has fewer than five real posts in the niche, publish the gap before applying. Write your traffic story in two honest sentences, naming the real platform and the real audience size.

Step 4. Apply. Keep a copy of what you submitted.

Step 5. Once approved, build one tracked link to one specific product, with a subID that names where you will use it. Record the parameter name the programme documentation specifies.

Step 6. Test it against the four point checklist: private window, correct landing page, affiliate ID intact after redirects, and click visible in the dashboard an hour later. Write down the result of each check.

Step 7. Start your programme record page: programme name, affiliate ID, login email, payout threshold, payment method, date joined. You will add to this for years.

If your application is rejected, write down the reason given and which of the four common causes it matches. Fix that one thing before reapplying.

quiz.question: Why add a subID such as subid=sewing-guide to your affiliate links?
options: It increases your commission rate
It lengthens the cookie window
It tells the dashboard which post or channel produced each click and sale
It is required before a programme will approve you

quiz.question: Your affiliate application is rejected. Which cause is most common for a first-time applicant?
options: Applying from Kenya rather than from abroad
Applying with an empty or near-empty site, before publishing real content in the niche
Asking for payment in shillings
Having fewer than 10,000 followers

lessons.title: Driving Traffic to Your Links
objectives: Tell the difference between browsing traffic and buyer-intent traffic, and write the kind of post that attracts the second
Choose a distribution channel that matches how your readers actually use the internet and what their data costs
Avoid the link-sharing behaviour that gets accounts banned and affiliate IDs removed
lessons.notes:
Traffic is the part people underestimate. Joining a programme takes an afternoon. Getting the right people to read you takes months. The good news is that only a small part of traffic work matters, and most beginners spend their time on the other part.

TWO KINDS OF TRAFFIC, AND ONLY ONE PAYS WELL

BROWSING traffic is somebody scrolling. They are not looking for your product, they are passing time. Browsing traffic is easy to get and converts terribly, often below 0.5 percent.

BUYER INTENT traffic is somebody who has already decided to buy something and is choosing between options. They typed a question into a search box. They asked a group for a recommendation. Intent traffic is much harder to get and converts five to twenty times better.

Nearly all the affiliate income in the world comes from intent traffic. Which means your job is not to be seen by as many people as possible. It is to be found by the few people who are deciding right now.

THE ONE POST SHAPE THAT EARNS

The highest-earning affiliate post is almost always a comparison for a reader with a constraint. Its title looks like one of these:

- "Best sewing machines under KSh 25,000 in Kenya (2026)"
- "Jumia vs Kilimall for buying a laptop: which is cheaper after delivery"
- "Hostinger or Namecheap for a small Kenyan business site"
- "Is the Tecno Spark worth it for a parent who only uses WhatsApp"

Three things make this shape work. It names a real decision. It includes the constraint, usually budget or location. And it promises a conclusion, not a list.

Inside the post, do what a friend would do:

- Recommend ONE option clearly, for a stated reason
- Name who should pick each alternative instead
- State the total real cost, including delivery, which most reviews ignore
- Say what the product is bad at. This is the single thing that most increases trust, and trust is what converts
- Put your link where the decision happens, next to the recommendation, not only at the bottom

WHERE KENYAN READERS WILL ACTUALLY FIND YOU

Pick channels on evidence about your readers, not on what is fashionable.

SEARCH is the best long-term source of intent traffic, and the slowest. A new post typically takes three to six months to collect steady search traffic, and your first ten posts may collect almost none. This is normal and it is the reason most people quit at week six. Search traffic also keeps arriving for years after you write the post, which no social post does.

WHATSAPP AND TELEGRAM COMMUNITIES are strong in Kenya when the community is YOURS and is about the topic. A group of 400 tailors who joined to talk about sewing is high intent. The same link pasted into a family group is not.

YOUTUBE works well for anything physical, because people want to see the item before paying. Note the data cost to your audience: a viewer on a daily bundle may not watch a twenty minute review. Short, direct videos respect that.

SHORT-FORM VIDEO on TikTok and Reels is good at reach and poor at intent. It can build an audience you later send to a comparison post. Treat it as the top of the path, not as the place the sale happens.

AN EMAIL OR BROADCAST LIST is the only audience you own. Platforms change their rules and your reach collapses overnight; a list does not. If your niche has repeat buying, start collecting contacts early, with permission, and note that collecting personal data brings obligations covered in the next lesson.

WHAT GETS YOUR ACCOUNTS CLOSED

This is where beginners lose everything they built:

- SPRAYING LINKS INTO GROUPS YOU DID NOT BUILD. It is the fastest way to be reported, removed, and sometimes to have your affiliate account terminated for spam, losing unpaid commission with it.
- LINKS IN PLACES THAT FORBID THEM. Some platforms strip or penalise outbound affiliate links. Read the platform rules, not just the programme rules.
- HIDING THAT A LINK IS AFFILIATE. Covered fully in the next lesson. It breaks both platform rules and consumer protection expectations.
- BIDDING ON THE BRAND NAME IN PAID ADS. Most programmes ban it outright because you are charging them for a customer who was already theirs.
- FAKE URGENCY AND INVENTED REVIEWS. Readers detect it, and a reversed reputation does not come back.

A PLAN FOR THE FIRST NINETY DAYS

Resist doing everything. A workable first quarter looks like this:

- Publish one comparison post a week in your niche. Twelve posts by day ninety.
- Share each one ONCE in a community where it is genuinely on topic and allowed.
- Answer questions in that community every week without posting links, so people know who you are.
- Collect contacts from readers who ask for more.
- Change nothing about strategy until day ninety, because search traffic has not had time to speak.

At day ninety, look at your subID data and see which single post earns. Then write three more posts like that one and stop doing the things that earned nothing.
lessons.practice:
Write one buyer-intent post and plan its distribution honestly.

Step 1. Write the title. Use the shape PRODUCT TYPE plus CONSTRAINT plus PLACE, for example "Best blenders under KSh 6,000 in Kenya". The constraint is not optional, it is the part that signals intent.

Step 2. Outline the post in seven lines, one line each:

- The decision the reader is stuck on
- Option one, and who should pick it
- Option two, and who should pick it
- Option three, and who should pick it
- Your single clear recommendation, with the reason
- Total real cost including delivery to a town outside Nairobi
- What your recommendation is BAD at

Step 3. Mark exactly where your affiliate link goes. There should be one next to the recommendation.

Step 4. Write your distribution plan with real names, not categories:

- The one community or platform where this post is genuinely on topic: ____
- Whether its rules permit affiliate links, and where you verified that: ____
- How many people will realistically see it: ____
- Expected clicks at 3 percent: ____
- Expected sales at 2 percent of clicks: ____

Step 5. Write the subID you will attach to this link so you can identify its clicks later.

Step 6. Answer one question in writing: if this post earns nothing in its first month, what will you conclude? If your answer is "the niche does not work", reread the section on how long search traffic takes. One month is not evidence.

quiz.question: Which reader is most likely to earn you a commission?
options: Someone scrolling TikTok who sees your product clip
Someone in your family WhatsApp group where you pasted a link
Someone who searched for the best blender under 6000 in Kenya and found your comparison
Someone who follows your page but has never read a post

quiz.question: You publish your first ten posts and after six weeks search traffic is almost zero. What does this most likely mean?
options: The niche has no demand and you should switch
Your links are broken
Nothing yet, because search traffic typically takes three to six months to build
You need to post the links into more WhatsApp groups

lessons.title: Disclosure & Compliance
objectives: Write a disclosure that a reader actually sees, and place it where the rules and common sense both require
Name the Kenyan obligations that attach to affiliate work: honest representations, personal data, and tax on the income
Recognise the programme terms that get affiliates removed, and check current requirements with the relevant authority instead of assuming
lessons.notes:
Disclosure is not a legal formality bolted onto affiliate marketing. It is the thing that makes the recommendation trustworthy, and trust is what converts. Readers who learn later that you were paid feel misled and stop reading. Readers who knew from the start and bought anyway are the ones who come back.

THE DISCLOSURE ITSELF

A good disclosure is short, plain, and impossible to miss:

"Some links below are affiliate links. If you buy through them I earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. It does not change what I recommend."

Three rules about it:

- PLACE IT ABOVE THE FIRST LINK, not in the footer and not at the end of a twelve minute video. A disclosure the reader meets after the decision is not a disclosure.
- WRITE IT IN PLAIN LANGUAGE. Not "this post may contain monetised third-party referral mechanisms".
- REPEAT IT WHERE THE CONTEXT CHANGES. In a video, say it aloud near the start AND put it in the description. In a WhatsApp message, include it in the same message as the link, because people forward single messages out of context.

WHAT YOU MAY NOT SAY, UNDER KENYAN LAW

Kenyan consumer protection law prohibits false or misleading representations about goods and services. In practice that means affiliate content must not:

- Claim you tested something you did not test
- State a price, a discount or an availability you have not verified
- Invent reviews or testimonials
- Manufacture urgency, such as a deadline that does not exist
- Omit a cost the reader will definitely pay, such as delivery or a mandatory subscription

The safest working rule is simple: everything you state as fact must be something you can show a source for, and everything else must be clearly framed as your opinion.

IF YOU COLLECT EMAILS OR PHONE NUMBERS

The moment you build a list, you are handling other people's personal data, and Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 applies to that. At minimum you need to:

- Collect with genuine consent, not by adding people who never asked
- Tell people what you will use their contact for, in a privacy notice on your site
- Make unsubscribing easy and honour it
- Keep the list somewhere access-controlled, not in a shared document
- Not sell or pass the list on without consent

There are registration requirements for data controllers and processors, with thresholds and exemptions that have changed since the Act commenced. Do not take a figure from a blog post, including this one. CHECK THE CURRENT REQUIREMENTS DIRECTLY WITH THE OFFICE OF THE DATA PROTECTION COMMISSIONER before you assume you are exempt.

TAX ON AFFILIATE INCOME

Affiliate commission is income. It is taxable whether it arrives in shillings to a Kenyan bank or in dollars to a payment account abroad, because Kenyan residents are taxed on income including foreign-sourced income. Several things follow:

- Keep records from your first payment: date, programme, gross commission, fees deducted, net received, exchange rate used
- Expect to declare this income in your annual return on iTax
- Which regime applies to you depends on your total turnover and how you are registered, and the thresholds for turnover tax and for VAT registration move

So treat the obligation as certain and the details as something to confirm. CHECK THE CURRENT THRESHOLDS AND YOUR OWN POSITION WITH KRA, or with an accountant, rather than relying on what somebody posted in a group. The expensive version of this mistake is discovering three years of undeclared income at once.

PROGRAMME TERMS THAT GET AFFILIATES REMOVED

Breaching these usually means termination AND forfeiting unpaid commission, which is why they belong in the same lesson as the law:

- SELF-REFERRAL. Buying through your own link, or asking family to use it for purchases they were making anyway. Programmes detect this through matching addresses and payment details.
- COUPON AND DISCOUNT ABUSE. Posing as a coupon site, or inserting your link late in somebody else's sale.
- BRAND-TERM BIDDING. Paying for ads on the company name, charging them for customers they already had.
- COOKIE STUFFING. Setting affiliate cookies without a click. This is fraud, not a grey area.
- UNAUTHORISED CLAIMS. Describing yourself as an official partner, or using logos in ways the terms forbid.
- MISLEADING LINK CLOAKING. Shortening links is normally fine; disguising an affiliate link as something else is not.

Read your programme terms once, properly, and keep a copy. They change, and the version that applies is the current one.

WHAT GOOD PRACTICE LOOKS LIKE IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Say plainly that you earn a commission, before the link. Only state facts you can support. Recommend what you would recommend unpaid, and say when a cheaper option is better even though it pays you less. Collect contact details only with consent and keep them safe. Record every shilling you earn and declare it. Read the programme terms. None of this costs you income; the last one just protects the income you already have.
lessons.practice:
Make your own compliance real rather than theoretical.

Step 1. Write your disclosure sentence in your own words. Keep it under 30 words and read it aloud. If it sounds like a contract, rewrite it.

Step 2. Decide and write down exactly where it will appear in each format you use: blog post, video, WhatsApp message, social caption. For each, note whether it sits ABOVE the first link.

Step 3. Audit one piece of content you have already published, or the post you outlined in lesson 4. Go through it line by line and mark every factual claim. For each, write the source. Any claim with no source gets rewritten as an opinion or removed.

Step 4. If you collect or plan to collect emails or phone numbers, write a four line privacy notice: what you collect, why, how long you keep it, and how somebody can be removed. Then write one line stating the date you will check current registration requirements with the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner.

Step 5. Start your income record now, before you earn anything. Make a page with these columns: date, programme, gross commission, fees, net received, currency and rate, and a note of which post earned it. Write one line stating what you will confirm with KRA about declaring this income.

Step 6. Open your programme terms. Find and copy out the clauses on self-referral, coupon sites, paid search and cookie handling. Write one sentence per clause saying what it means for what you plan to do.

If any step above shows that something you are already doing breaches a rule, fix that today rather than after a payout is withheld.

quiz.question: Where does an affiliate disclosure belong?
options: In the site footer, where it covers every page at once
Above the first affiliate link, in plain language the reader meets before deciding
At the end of the post, so it does not discourage clicks
Only in the programme terms you agreed to

quiz.question: You are about to start collecting reader email addresses for a monthly recommendation list. What is the correct next step regarding Kenyan data protection rules?
options: Assume you are exempt, because you are an individual rather than a company
Use a figure from an affiliate marketing blog to decide whether to register
Collect with consent, publish a privacy notice, and check current registration requirements directly with the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner
Nothing applies until the list passes 1,000 subscribers

lessons.title: Tracking Your Earnings
objectives: Track the four numbers that explain affiliate performance, and tell pending commission apart from money that has actually arrived
Account for the gap between a dashboard figure and a bank balance: reversals, thresholds, currency conversion and transfer fees
Use subID data to decide what to repeat and what to stop, on evidence rather than on feel
lessons.notes:
Affiliate dashboards are designed to be encouraging. They show you clicks and gross commission in large type, because those numbers always look better than what reaches your account. Tracking your own figures is how you find out what is really happening.

THE FOUR NUMBERS, IN ORDER

Record these monthly, per programme:

1. CLICKS. How many people clicked an affiliate link.
2. CONVERSIONS. How many of those bought. Conversions divided by clicks is your conversion rate, and it tells you whether your traffic has buying intent.
3. GROSS COMMISSION. What the dashboard says you earned, before anything is deducted or reversed.
4. NET RECEIVED. What actually landed in your bank or payment account, after reversals, thresholds, conversion and fees.

Most people track only the first and third. The interesting information is in the difference between the third and the fourth.

PENDING, APPROVED, REVERSED

Commission passes through states, and only one of them is money:

- PENDING. A sale was recorded. Nothing is owed yet.
- APPROVED. The programme has confirmed it after its return and fraud window, often 30 to 60 days.
- REVERSED. The sale was cancelled, returned, unpaid, or judged invalid. The commission disappears from your balance.

A reversal rate of 5 to 15 percent is ordinary for physical goods, where people return things. For software it is usually lower, but refund guarantees still bite.

So never spend a pending balance, and never report pending figures as earnings. Judge a month only after its approval window has closed.

WHY THE DASHBOARD AND THE BANK DISAGREE

Four things stand between gross commission and your account:

- REVERSALS, as above.
- THE PAYOUT THRESHOLD. Below it, nothing is sent and the balance rolls over. A 100 dollar threshold on 12 dollars a month means your first payment arrives in month nine.
- CURRENCY CONVERSION. Dollars become shillings at a rate chosen by whoever converts them, usually a little worse than the mid-market rate.
- TRANSFER AND WITHDRAWAL FEES. A fixed fee hurts small payouts most. A flat 5 dollar fee on a 30 dollar payout is 17 percent of your income.

This is why a local programme paying 7 percent in shillings to a Kenyan bank can beat an international one paying 30 percent in dollars, at small volumes. Run that comparison with your own numbers rather than assuming the bigger percentage wins.

SUBIDS TURN GUESSING INTO MANAGING

If you tagged your links as lesson 3 described, your dashboard can tell you which post or channel produced each click and each sale. This is the most useful data you have, because affiliate earnings are almost never spread evenly. The usual pattern is that one or two pieces of content produce most of the income and everything else produces nearly nothing.

That pattern is instruction, not disappointment. It tells you exactly what to write more of.

Look for three things in subID data:

- The post with the best CONVERSION RATE, not the most clicks. High clicks with no sales means browsing traffic. Few clicks with several sales means you found intent, and should write three more like it.
- The channel that produces clicks that never convert. That is where your time is being spent for nothing.
- The product with an unusually high reversal rate. Readers are buying and sending it back, which means your post is overselling it. Fix the post.

A SHEET YOU WILL ACTUALLY KEEP

Complicated tracking gets abandoned in month two. One spreadsheet with these columns is enough:

Month, programme, subID, clicks, conversions, conversion rate, gross commission, reversals, approved, net received, currency and rate used, notes.

Fill it in once a month, on a fixed date. Copy the figures from the programme dashboard rather than from memory. Keep the same sheet for years, because the trend over twelve months tells you far more than any single month.

That sheet is also your tax record, which is the second reason to keep it properly. Gross commission, fees and net received are exactly the figures a return or an accountant will ask for.

THE NINETY DAY DECISION

After ninety days of real traffic, not before, make one decision per piece of content and one per channel:

- REPEAT. It converted. Write more like it.
- FIX. It got clicks but no sales. The traffic is wrong or the post oversells. Change one thing and give it another cycle.
- STOP. Ninety days of genuine effort, meaningful clicks, and no conversions. Stop and move the time to what worked.

Set a date for this review now, and write it down. Without a fixed date the easy thing is to keep doing everything for another year, which is how people spend two years earning KSh 400 a month.

WHEN TO CHECK WHETHER SOMETHING IS BROKEN

Clicks with zero conversions over a long stretch is sometimes bad traffic and sometimes a broken link. Before concluding anything about your audience, retest the link with the four point check from lesson 3. Silent link breakage after a site change is common and costs people months.
lessons.practice:
Build the tracking sheet and record an honest baseline.

Step 1. Make a spreadsheet with these exact columns: Month, Programme, SubID, Clicks, Conversions, Conversion rate, Gross commission, Reversals, Approved, Net received, Currency and rate, Notes.

Step 2. Fill in one row per subID from whatever data you have today, even if every number is zero. A baseline of zeros dated today is more useful than a perfect sheet started in six months.

Step 3. From your programme dashboard, find and write down three facts: your current pending balance, your current approved balance, and the date of your next scheduled payment. Note which of the two balances is actually money.

Step 4. Work out your real cost of getting paid. Take your current or expected monthly commission and calculate:

- Months to reach the payout threshold: ____
- Expected currency conversion loss: ____
- Fixed transfer or withdrawal fee: ____
- Fees as a percentage of that payout: ____

If fees exceed 10 percent, write one sentence on what you would change: fewer, larger payouts, a different payment method, or a programme that pays in shillings.

Step 5. Pick the date, ninety days from today, for your repeat-fix-stop review. Write the actual date. Write the one rule you will apply at that review: any channel with meaningful clicks and zero conversions gets stopped.

Step 6. Set a monthly reminder to fill in the sheet on a fixed day. Then compare today's row with the earnings estimate you calculated in lesson 1 and write one sentence about the difference. Whichever direction it went, that gap is the most accurate thing you now know about your own audience.

quiz.question: Your dashboard shows KSh 8,400 pending and KSh 1,200 approved. What have you earned?
options: KSh 9,600, since both figures are commission
KSh 8,400, because pending commission is the newer figure
KSh 1,200, because only approved commission has cleared the return and fraud window
Nothing until the full amount is paid out

quiz.question: SubID data shows post A with 900 clicks and no sales, and post B with 60 clicks and 4 sales. What is the right response?
options: Promote post A harder, since it clearly attracts the most interest
Write more content like post B, and investigate whether post A attracts browsing traffic or has a broken link
Delete both and change niche
Treat them as equal, because total clicks matter more than conversions
